textBoxes.text: Fractals are by far my favorite topic to explore in p5.js. Here, I have explored four different techniques to generate fractals.

Computational randomness formed the basis of my first encounter with generative art.

My creative coding explorations have consistently centered on systems that incorporate elements of randomness, rather than fully deterministic compositions.

I was introduced to the work of artist *Desmond Paul Henry*[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Paul_Henry] in the first p5.js class I took in 2018.

He used WW2 bomb sight computers to create mechanical randomness. His contraptions physcally plotted complex patterns.

In this section I implemented the basic walker class.

Randomly picks a direction moves in that direction per frame

Extended the walker class to support color.
 
Experimented with rendering multiple walkers.

The blur filter is my favourite. 

Whenever I feel uninspired I just experiment with the blur filter.

I wanted to explore multiples axis of randomness in this composition.
 
I started by randomly plotting points on the canvas.

I implemented non uniform randomness to spawn points more towards the centre. 

I wanted to explore how the walker could interact with the points. Everytime a walker hits a point it should activate.
I am taking a class with the *Ken Perlin*[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Perlin] himself. I had to implement Perlin noise in some way!
I experimented with different kinds of walkers and different visual variations of the points activation

I remember struggling with vectors when they were taught as part of mathematics in high school. I also remember avoiding vectors in my p5.js sketches, often opting instead for trigonometric or algebraic approaches to motion.

However, once I got the hang of them, vectors became one of the most powerful tools in my creative coding palette.

Started with the basic bouncing ball example from the book. 

Experimented with systems with gravity and without.
Explored methods to smoothen motion. Created a ball class that follows the cursor
I tried out different ways in which the ways in which the "following" object could render.
I also turn to grids whenever I’m lacking inspiration. For this implementation, I abstracted the Ball class so that it could operate within a Cell class.
Experimented with offset of position and randomization of inital state of each cell

What if the cell class itself became a perlin walker? 

experimented with the cell class to create some interesting effects. Very paintbrush like
Blur just makes everthing more intersting. A very water shader-esque outcome
This week I explored forces as vectors: quantities with both direction and magnitude. Making the vectors visible helped me understand how acceleration changes a mover's velocity over time.
I built a reusable Mover class around position, velocity, and acceleration. Separating this logic made it much easier to apply the same forces to one object or an entire system of movers.

I converted Perlin noise into angles, then used those angles to build a vector field. The continuous noise creates a flow that feels organic while still giving every point in the grid a clear direction.
The movers sample the vector beneath them and apply it as a force. Their paths reveal the invisible field, turning a grid of arrows into a moving particle system.

When many movers followed the same field they began to clump together. I added a short-range separation force so nearby particles push away from one another while continuing to follow the larger flow.
For oscillation, I wanted to move beyond drawing a single sine wave. I used periodic values as controls that could drive position, rotation, scale, and color across a larger composition.
I started by creating a Tile class that could contain a small animation. This gave me one reusable unit to repeat, offset, and combine without rewriting the drawing logic.
Once the tiles were arranged in a grid, I offset the phase of each cell. A small change in timing creates waves that travel horizontally, diagonally, or outward from the center.
The radial offset was especially interesting because distance from the center became a timing value. The grid stopped reading as separate cells and began behaving like one surface.
I moved the oscillation logic into each tile so that position, rotation, and shape could be varied independently. This made the later experiments much easier to compose.
The final compositions combine several simple periodic systems. I explored polygons, lava-lamp-like motion, and color changes to see how far the same oscillation structure could stretch visually.

Particle systems shifted my focus from controlling one object to designing rules for a population. The individual particles are simple; the visual complexity comes from emission, lifespan, forces, and accumulation.
I separated the system into Particle and Emitter classes. The emitter manages when and where particles are born, while each particle carries its own motion and lifespan.
Extending particle lifespan made the flow field easier to read because each path remained visible for longer. It also made performance and cleanup more important as the population grew.
A direct anti-clumping check compares every particle with every other particle and quickly becomes expensive. I introduced spatial hashing so each particle only checks nearby grid cells.
I turned the emitter itself into a Perlin walker. The source now drifts through the canvas, and using multiple walkers creates overlapping streams instead of a single fixed fountain.
Random color created energy but very little cohesion. Fixing a palette gave the system a stronger identity while still allowing variation at the moment each particle is emitted.
Blur and translucent trails turn particle movement into texture. I eventually connected the system to camera input, letting live sampled colors enter the same force-based drawing process.
My first L-system uses a short grammar to replace symbols over multiple generations. Angle, segment length, and generation depth become compact controls for surprisingly complex branching structures.
Mapping the mouse and sine functions to angle and length made the grammar feel less static. The underlying rules stay the same while the rendered structure continuously changes character.
I adapted the L-system into bamboo by separating the fixed stem from generative leaves. This was an exercise in using formal rules toward a recognizable visual subject rather than pure abstraction.
For the recursive drawing tool, each frame can contain shapes and render other frames. The frame becomes both a composition boundary and a reusable instruction inside a deeper render pass.
As the recursive frame experiment grew, I added multiple frames, a better brush, undo, hideable controls, and saved configuration. The sketch gradually became a small drawing tool.
The chaos game creates structure by repeatedly moving a point partway toward a randomly selected anchor. Local random choices eventually reveal a stable global form such as the Sierpiński triangle.
I varied anchor count, step size, rotation, and selection rules. Restrictions such as not repeating an anchor transform the attractor, showing how small rule changes reshape the entire system.
Rendering the Mandelbrot set began with mapping pixels onto the complex plane. Each pixel records whether repeated iteration escapes, translating an invisible mathematical process into an image.
I added smooth coloring, zoom, adaptive iteration counts, and saved render settings. Color is based on escape behavior, so the palette exposes subtle differences around the set's boundary.
For the midterm I explored emergence through Conway's Game of Life. Each cell follows a tiny local rule, yet the grid produces motion, repetition, growth, and collapse without a central controller.
I began with a Cell class and then organized the cells into a grid. Keeping state inside each cell made the larger simulation easier to update and render consistently.
Every generation is calculated from the eight neighboring cells. Birth, survival, and death are simple Boolean decisions, but they create patterns that appear almost intentional.
Mouse interaction lets me activate cells and interrupt the simulation's current state. Instead of only observing emergence, I can seed a pattern and watch how the system responds.
After the rules were working, I explored color, glyphs, neon, sound reactivity, and a blood-cell variation. The same cellular logic can support many different visual identities.
